title: Recovery, quarantine, blast radius and bulk operations
summary: The recovery ladder repairs devices underneath live leases. It reads farm.leases in exactly one function, only to decide whether it is allowed to act, and no code path in internal/recovery writes one. Every rung declares a blast radius and the minimum disruption_policy a live lease in that radius must carry; a rung that would reach a lease forbidding it is refused outright, recorded in farm.recovery_attempts.refusal, and the device stays broken until the work on it ends. Three things will cost you a night if you do not read the gaps first: host drain is not enforced by the allocator, tiers 3 and 4 cannot execute in any shipped deployment, and closing a quarantine does nothing unless the recovery loop is running.

sections.heading: What recovery may and may not do
sections.body:
Recovery acts **on behalf of** a lease holder while the holder keeps its device. The lease clock keeps ticking, the fence never moves, and the job is told what is happening. Nothing in `internal/recovery` ends a lease.

The enforcement is the import list, not a convention: the package does not import `internal/lease`, so `lease_release` and `lease_reclaim` are out of scope in every function in it. It touches `farm.leases` in exactly one place — `checkBlastRadius` — and reads exactly two things there: that a lease exists, and what `disruption_policy` it carries. The only direction that information flows is toward **refusing to act**.

The same rule holds one level down. `internal/node` has no lease vocabulary either: a device it power-cycles is very probably three hours into somebody's job, and repairing the USB link under a live lease is the entire point of tiers 3 and 4.

A stopped ladder is safe. `Ladder.Run` logs `recovery ladder stopping; no lease was ever at risk from it` and returns nil on cancellation. Broken devices stay broken, which is inconvenient; nothing is taken from anybody.
bullets: `farm.recovery_attempts.outcome` has five values — recovered, no_change, failed, refused, aborted. None of them means "gave up and took the device back".

The recovery loop's heartbeat (`farm.component_heartbeat` key `recovery`) must NOT be listed in `FARM_REAPER_COMPONENTS`. `farm.reaper_arm` adds the named components' downtime to every live lease's `expires_at` and `reclaimable_at`; putting the health plane in that list would let a recovery outage move lease clocks. The shipped default is `{reaper, api, scheduler}` (`internal/config/config.go:124`), and the live farm's heartbeat table shows `recovery`, `watchdog:h01` and `watchdog:h02` correctly outside it.

`no_change` folds to `failed` in the obs metrics on purpose (`obsOutcome`): "the action ran and nothing changed" is not a recovery, and a false `recovered` suppresses the page that should have followed.

sections.heading: The ladder, rung by rung
sections.body:
The nine rungs live in `farm.recovery_tiers`, not in code. The ladder re-reads the table **every cycle** (default 15s) rather than caching it, so an operator can retune budgets without a redeploy and `GET /api/v1/recovery` can show what the system will try before it tries it.

`blast_radius` is what else the rung disturbs. `requires_policy` is the minimum `disruption_policy` every live lease inside that radius must carry. `cooldown` and `max_per_hour` are evaluated **in the blast radius scope**, not per device — a per-device count would let one hub absorb eight `adb_restart`s an hour by spreading them across eight devices.

Where each rung executes:

- **0, 6, 8** (observe, quarantine, host_drain) are database actions the ladder performs itself. They never reach an actuator.
- **1, 2, 5, 7** (adb_reconnect, transport_reset, device_reboot, adb_restart) are ADB verbs performed by `ADBActuator` through the host's ADB server.
- **3, 4** (usb_reset, port_power) need a process on the host itself. See the gaps: no shipped deployment has one.

Every hardware address is a **position** (`farm.slots.adb_devpath`, `usb:3-1.4` form), never a serial. Duplicate OEM serials are real; a recovery addressed by serial can land on a healthy device holding a live six-hour lease.
bullets: `next(tiers, cur)` returns the first rung with `tier > cur`. A device that exhausts the ladder **repeats its top rung**, bounded by that rung's own cooldown and cap — a six-hourly `host_drain` on repeat is the ladder saying "still broken, still needs a human".
Tier 7 (`adb_restart`) has blast radius `host` because killing the ADB server severs every device on that host. It is the only ADB-reachable rung with a host-wide radius.

Tier 8 (`host_drain`) opens a host-scoped quarantine and marks every device on the host `quarantined`. It deliberately does **not** write `farm.hosts.admin_state` — and given that nothing enforces `draining` (see gaps), the quarantine is the only part of a drain that actually stops allocation.

sections.heading: Why a rung is refused rather than downgraded
sections.body:
When the ladder picks a rung, the **first** thing it does — before any state change — is ask what that rung would disturb and whether every live lease in that scope permits it. If not, the rung is refused. Not downgraded to a cheaper one, not deferred silently, not performed anyway.

The reason is the trade: a phone is worth less than six hours of somebody's test run. Downgrading would mean the ladder quietly does something weaker and then escalates again on the same evidence; performing anyway is DeviceFarmer/STF #663.

`policyRank` orders the three policies least- to most-permissive: `no_disruption` < `allow_soft_reset` < `allow_port_power_cycle`. A rung is allowed only when **every** live lease in its radius ranks at or above the rung's `requires_policy`.

Two widenings make the check conservative:

- A tier with `blast_radius = 'power_domain'` whose slot has **no** `power_domain_id` is widened to `hub`. Unknown power topology is not per-port topology; the widening can only ever cause a refusal.
- The refusal distinguishes *this device's own lease* from *a neighbour in the same radius*, and a neighbour on a `ganged` power domain is tagged `refused_ganged` in metrics — because a rising rate there means the rack needs per-port switching, not that the ladder is broken. Note that this tag has never actually been emitted on this demo; see gaps.

Be careful about which refusal you are reading. There are three distinct producers of `farm.recovery_attempts.refusal` in this tree, with three different message formats: the ladder's `checkBlastRadius`, the API's `handleSlotPower`, and the demo simulator's `escalationRefusal`. Only the first two are production code.
bullets: Refusals are **written**, not skipped: `farm.recovery_attempts` gets a row with `outcome='refused'` and the reason in `refusal`. "Nothing happened here" and "we declined to act, and here is why" must not look the same at 3am.

A refusal does **not** consume the rung's hourly budget — the budget CTE filters `outcome IS DISTINCT FROM 'refused'`. A device can be refused tier 4 all day and still get a real tier 4 the moment the lease ends.

An unrecognised `disruption_policy` value is treated as restrictive in both implementations, but not identically. `recovery.policyRank` ranks it 0, the same as `no_disruption`, so it still permits the four tiers that require `no_disruption`. `api.policyRank` ranks it 0 against `no_disruption`'s 1, so it is strictly below every tier. Adding a fourth policy value means editing both, and reconciling that difference.

examples.label: Refusals do not spend budget — the ladder's own accounting, run against power domain 3
examples.code:
WITH att AS (
  SELECT a.started_at, a.outcome
    FROM farm.recovery_attempts a
    LEFT JOIN farm.slots s ON s.id = a.slot_id
   WHERE a.tier = 4 AND s.power_domain_id = 3
     AND a.started_at > now() - interval '1 hour')
SELECT count(*) AS all_tier4_last_hour,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE outcome IS DISTINCT FROM 'refused') AS counted_against_budget
  FROM att;

sections.heading: Budgets: cooldown, hourly cap, and the per-device lock
sections.body:
After the blast-radius check passes, one short transaction takes a per-device advisory lock, re-checks three budgets under it, opens the attempt row, and suppresses health writes. The transaction deliberately does **not** wrap the action itself: a uhubctl cycle can take a minute, and holding a transaction across it pins a pool connection and a lock for the duration.

The three ways an attempt is skipped before it starts:

1. **in_flight** — an attempt on this device is still open (`finished_at IS NULL`) and younger than `StaleAttempt` (15m). Two ladders on one phone is how a reset lands in the middle of the next reset. After 15 minutes an unfinished attempt is assumed dead — the process was killed mid-action — and stops blocking. This check keys on `device_id`, so an attempt row with a NULL device (everything `handleSlotPower` writes) never blocks anything.
2. **cooldown** — an attempt at this tier, in this blast-radius scope, inside the tier's `cooldown`.
3. **max_per_hour** — count of non-refused attempts at this tier in this scope over the last hour, against the tier's cap. Repeating a tier that is not working is how a farm power-cycles a hub forty times an hour.

The lock is `pg_advisory_xact_lock`, keyed on `hashtext(device_id)` with class `26981`. Transaction-scoped rather than session-scoped so `COMMIT` releases it even if the process dies holding it.

On success, `begin` also writes `suppress_until = now() + LEAST(tier.cooldown, MaxSuppress)` where `MaxSuppress` is 3 minutes, and moves health to `recovering` unless the device is already `quarantined` or `retired`. The suppression stops the watchdog from recording an **induced** transport drop as a fresh fault and re-arming the whole ladder. It is capped at 3 minutes on purpose: letting a 15-minute tier cooldown suppress health for 15 minutes would hide a real fault.
bullets: Scope matters. Tier 7 (`adb_restart`, radius `host`, cap 1/hour) is one restart per host per hour, no matter how many devices on that host are sick.
Health is frozen while `suppress_until` is open, so the candidate query requires `updated_at > suppress_until` — waiting only for the window to lapse would spend the next rung on the frozen value.

`finish` writes on a context detached from the loop's, so an attempt that ran is recorded even during shutdown. Otherwise the next process sees an unfinished attempt and blocks that device for 15 minutes.

examples.label: The exact budget query the ladder runs, for tier 4 on power domain 1
examples.code:
WITH att AS (
  SELECT a.started_at
    FROM farm.recovery_attempts a
    LEFT JOIN farm.slots s ON s.id = a.slot_id
   WHERE a.tier = 4
     AND a.outcome IS DISTINCT FROM 'refused'
     AND a.started_at > now() - GREATEST(interval '10 minutes', interval '1 hour')
     AND s.power_domain_id = 1)
SELECT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM att WHERE started_at > now() - interval '10 minutes') AS in_cooldown,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM att WHERE started_at > now() - interval '1 hour') AS in_hour,
       4 AS max_per_hour;
examples.note: in_hour is 2 because two operator-requested tier-4 attempts on this domain were approved and never closed. They are not refusals, so they count. They age out after an hour — the cost is real but time-bounded, not permanent. See the gap about attempt rows nothing closes.

sections.heading: Which devices the ladder will even look at
sections.body:
`candidates` is deliberately narrow. Three predicates exist so the loop acts only on evidence the health plane currently vouches for.

- **`health NOT IN ('healthy','retired','quarantined','unknown')`.** `unknown` means nobody has looked — it is what a fresh `farm.device_runtime` row carries and what `reconcileQuarantines` writes to every device of a quarantine an operator just closed. Climbing a ladder on it is escalating against the *absence* of evidence.
- **`adb_state <> 'device'`.** That value means the ADB server is talking to the device right now; there is no transport left to repair. A device can sit at health `recovering` with a good transport for minutes, because promotion back to `healthy` costs the watchdog's `consec_good` hysteresis plus a flap token — deliberately slower than the ladder's cooldowns. Without this predicate the ladder outruns the damper and climbs from a reconnect that *worked* to a power cycle and then a quarantine, against a device that is already back.
- **`suppress_until` lapsed AND `updated_at > suppress_until`.** See the previous section.

On top of that: `health_since` older than the debounce (45s), device `admin_state='enabled'`, slot `state='active'`, host **not `disabled`** — note that a `draining` host's devices remain recovery candidates, which is correct: a drain is about allocation, not repair — and **no open quarantine at any scope** covering the device, its slot, its hub or its host.

`farm.leases` is absent from this query on purpose. Whether a device is leased changes what the ladder may *do* to it, never whether it *looks* at it.

The 45-second debounce is why this demo almost never produces a per-device ladder climb: the simulator restores its offline devices inside that window, so they are healthy again before they qualify. Do not read the absence of tier-1-through-5 rows here as evidence those rungs work.

Consequence worth internalising: **with no watchdog running there is no confirmation and the ladder stalls.** A stalled ladder leaves broken devices broken. A ladder driven by a dead health plane power-cycles a working rack. The stall is the correct failure.

examples.label: Run the ladder's candidate query yourself. On a settled farm it is usually empty.
examples.code:
SELECT r.device_id::text, r.health, r.adb_state, r.ladder_tier, s.rack_slot, hb.usb_path, ho.id
  FROM farm.device_runtime r
  JOIN farm.devices d ON d.id = r.device_id
  JOIN farm.slots   s ON s.id = d.current_slot_id
  JOIN farm.hubs   hb ON hb.id = s.hub_id
  JOIN farm.hosts  ho ON ho.id = s.host_id
 WHERE r.health NOT IN ('healthy','retired','quarantined','unknown')
   AND r.adb_state <> 'device'
   AND r.health_since < now() - interval '45 seconds'
   AND (r.suppress_until IS NULL
        OR (r.suppress_until <= now() AND r.updated_at > r.suppress_until))
   AND d.admin_state = 'enabled' AND s.state = 'active' AND ho.admin_state <> 'disabled'
   AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM farm.quarantines q WHERE q.closed_at IS NULL
        AND (q.device_id = d.id OR q.slot_id = s.id OR q.hub_id = hb.id OR q.host_id = ho.id))
 ORDER BY r.health_since LIMIT 25;
examples.note: Run at a moment when farm.device_runtime held one `offline` and one `degraded` device. Neither qualified: both had a health_since three seconds old. Dropping the 45s predicate returns them. If you are debugging "why is the ladder not acting", remove one predicate at a time from this query — that is the whole decision.

sections.heading: The rungs that need a host agent, and what happens without one
sections.body:
Tiers 3 and 4 cannot be done over ADB:

- **tier 3, usb_reset** — `USBDEVFS_RESET` ioctl on `/dev/bus/usb/BBB/DDD`
- **tier 4, port_power** — toggling VBUS through the hub with `uhubctl`

Both need a process with the host's own filesystem and hub. That process is `farmd-node` (`internal/node`), which implements `recovery.HostRunner`.

When `ADBActuator.HostRunner` is nil, those rungs are **refused with a reason naming what is missing**, never faked. The doc comment is explicit about why: reporting `no_change` for a rung nobody attempted teaches the ladder the hardware is unrecoverable and gets a healthy device quarantined.

The refusal text is:

> tier 3 (usb_reset) needs USBDEVFS_RESET on host h01, which only a farmd-node agent can do; no host agent is configured for this farm

**Read the gaps before relying on any of this.** No shipped role wires a `HostRunner` into the ladder — `cmd/farmd/roles.go:206` constructs `recovery.NewADBActuator(log, nil)` unconditionally for `recovery`, `all` and `demo` alike, and no role runs the agent and the ladder in one process. In every deployment `farmd` currently offers, tiers 3 and 4 are refusals.

The agent's own surface, if you run it: three routes, all bearer-token gated including `GET /node/v1/health`, because health reports which epoch is in force and whether ADB is answering — exactly the reconnaissance an attacker wants before choosing a port to cut power to. `Handler()` refuses to construct at all without a token.

Two design points on that endpoint that matter under failure:

- `host_id` is **required** over HTTP. `usb:3-1.4` is a real port on every host in the fleet; a misrouted request would cut power to this rack because another rack was sick. The in-process seam may omit it because it reaches exactly one agent.
- Once accepted, the operation runs on a context **detached from the request**. A client hanging up mid-cycle does not abort a VBUS cycle mid-settle. The deadline is `opBudget()` = `CallTimeout (10s) + PowerOffSettle (3s) + PortReturnTimeout (30s) + DefaultOpGrace (30s)` = 73s by default — a decision rather than a socket.
bullets: `ErrRefused` maps to HTTP 409, `ErrNotSupported` to 501, anything else to 500. A 409 must not be retried unchanged.

The package's platform seam keeps `unsupportedPlatform` on any GOOS but Linux, so both hardware rungs answer with `ErrNotSupported` naming the platform. But the `farmd node` **role** never reaches it: `runNode` calls `topo.Sysfs("/sys")` first, which errors on non-Linux before an Agent exists.

The agent's heartbeat should be per host (`node:<host id>`), and the package default is. The shipped role passes `Component: "node"` explicitly and defeats it — see gaps. Either way it must not go in `FARM_REAPER_COMPONENTS`.

sections.heading: The kernel 6.0 floor, and why a cycle below it silently does nothing
sections.body:
Before Linux 6.0 the USB core **re-powers a port that was switched off behind its back**. `uhubctl` sends `CLEAR_FEATURE(PORT_POWER)`, the hub obeys, and the kernel turns the port straight back on. uhubctl reports success. The port never went dark. The device never saw a power cycle.

If that were reported as a completed rung, the ladder would learn that tier 4 was tried and did not help — and escalate to quarantining a device whose only real problem is that the one rung that would have fixed it was never actually performed.

So `checkKernelFloor` refuses the whole rung on kernel < 6.0, with a message naming something an operator can act on:

> this host runs kernel 5.15.0, and before 6.0 the USB core re-powers a port that was switched off, so the cycle would report success without the device ever losing power; upgrade the host kernel to make recovery tier 4 real here

A kernel release that cannot be **read** is also a refusal, for the same reason: the agent cannot tell whether a power-off would survive.

The version comes from `/proc/sys/kernel/osrelease`, not `uname(2)`. `syscall.Utsname.Release` is `[65]int8` on amd64 and `[65]uint8` on arm64, so a uname reader needs per-architecture conversion; the proc file is identical text everywhere. Only `major.minor` is parsed.
bullets: Even above 6.0, the cycle is **verified**, not assumed. If the device was enumerated before the cut, the agent waits up to 2s (`offVerifyWindow`) for it to disappear from sysfs; if it is still there, the error says outright that VBUS was not actually cut and tier 4 cannot work on this host.
If the device had already fallen off the bus — the ordinary reason to reach tier 4 — its absence during the off step proves nothing and is not treated as evidence either way.

`uhubctl` not on PATH is also a refusal, with the honest consequence spelled out: "install it or accept that this host's ladder stops at tier 3". A host agent normally runs from a unit file with a minimal PATH, so six install locations (`/usr/sbin`, `/usr/bin`, `/usr/local/sbin`, `/usr/local/bin`, `/sbin`, `/bin`) are checked before giving up.

sections.heading: The agent is the last line on blast radius
sections.body:
The control plane checked lease policy. The agent checks again, because it is the only party that can see what is **actually plugged into the hub at this instant**. On a ganged hub the difference between "cycle this port" and "cycle these seven ports" is invisible from the control plane.

`checkBlastRadius` builds an allow-set of the target plus everything in `acknowledged`, then walks every hub uhubctl reported:

- **per-port hub** (`ppps` in the descriptor): only this port's occupant is counted.
- **anything else** — `ganged`, or a descriptor that could not be parsed — every occupant is counted. Assuming per-port switching on a hub that does not have it is how one recovery action becomes seven broken jobs.

Occupancy comes from sysfs, not uhubctl's connect flags, because sysfs is the same namespace the rest of the farm addresses devices in. And it counts **descendants**: plug a hub into port 3 of `3-1.4` and the phones behind it are `3-1.4.3.1`, `3-1.4.3.2`… Acknowledging the hub is not acknowledging the phones. Each is a separate device that may hold a separate lease.

The location is passed to uhubctl **without `--exact`**. A USB3 receptacle appears to the kernel as two hubs — SuperSpeed plus a USB2 companion — and one physical port is one port on each. uhubctl's default duality handling switches both, which is what actually cuts power to the socket; `--exact` would switch one half and could leave a USB2 phone powered. The cost is that the true blast radius spans both hubs, which is why `readHubs` returns every hub uhubctl reported rather than only the one asked for.

**Power-on is the one step that retries.** The guard is armed *before* the port is switched off, not after, because uhubctl can fail partway — switch the USB3 hub, then error on the USB2 companion — so a non-zero exit is not evidence that power is still on. The only way out of `portPower` is through a power-on attempt, and that attempt runs on a context **detached** from the caller's: an expired deadline or a Ctrl-C is not a reason to leave a rack of phones dark. If it still fails, the log prints the exact `uhubctl -l <hub> -p <port> -a on` a human has to type, with the hub and port derived from `hubLocation()` on the slot's `usb_path`.
bullets: Refusal text is sorted, so the same refusal reads identically every time it lands in `farm.recovery_attempts`.

`readUSBNode` **reads** busnum and devnum from sysfs, never derives them. A devnum changes on every re-enumeration and bus numbers depend on controller probe order; guessing either eventually sends `USBDEVFS_RESET` to a different phone that is very likely holding a live lease.

`usbPathOf` enforces `^[0-9]+-[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)*$` — byte for byte the CHECK constraint on `farm.slots.usb_path` — admitting neither a slash nor a dot-dot. It is the only sanitisation these strings get before being joined onto `/sys` and `/dev`, and the next thing that happens to the value is a power cycle.
`acknowledged` is never populated by any caller in this tree, which makes tier 4 on ganged hardware unavailable through the in-process seam. See gaps.

sections.heading: Hub correlation: several devices failing together is ONE incident
sections.body:
Devices that fail together share hardware. When a majority of one hub's devices go bad inside a short window, the evidence is about the **hub** — a power brick, a controller, a cable to the host. Opening N device quarantines would produce N pages, N ladder climbs, and N power cycles that cannot fix a hub.

So `correlate` runs **before** any per-device escalation each cycle, opens one hub-scoped quarantine, and marks every device on that hub as handled so the per-device loop skips them.

The rule (`hubIsTheFault`), with shipped defaults:

- the hub has at least 2 devices,
- at least `MinHubBad` = 2 of them are unhealthy,
- a **strict** majority: `unhealthy > 0.5 * devices`,
- and the spread between first and last `health_since` is ≤ `HubWindow` = 3 minutes.

The window matters as much as the count. Six devices that failed over three days are six independent faults; six that failed inside three minutes are one fault upstream of all of them.

The numerator counts **only positive evidence of a fault** — `offline`, `unauthorized`, `missing`, `degraded`. Four states are excluded, each for a specific loop it would otherwise create:

- `unknown` — `reconcileQuarantines` writes it to *every* device on a hub, in one statement, the moment an operator closes that hub's quarantine. Same `health_since` for all of them, so the spread is zero and the quorum is unanimous. Counting it re-opens the quarantine the operator just closed, about a debounce window later, forever.
- `recovering` — this loop wrote it in `begin`. Two devices under active recovery on a three-device hub reach quorum and quarantine the healthy third.
- `quarantined` — our own bookkeeping, not a new observation.
- `booting` — authorizing/connecting is transient; a legitimate mass reboot would read as a hub fault.

The **denominator stays `count(*)`** over all the hub's devices, retired and healthy included. That only makes quorum harder, which is the safe direction for an action whose blast radius is a whole hub.

`farm.v_hub_health` does **not** use this definition. Its `unhealthy` column is `count(*) FILTER (WHERE r.health NOT IN ('healthy','retired'))`, so it counts quarantined, unknown and recovering devices too. The fleet banner and the quarantine reason will disagree about the same hub, by design of two separate queries — know which one you are reading.

Opening the quarantine is idempotent across replicas: an `INSERT ... WHERE NOT EXISTS` plus the partial unique index `q_open_hub` catch both the check-then-insert race and a lost race between replicas, and neither is reported as new. The recorded outcome is `no_change`, not `recovered`, because nothing was repaired: scheduling stopped and a human was told.

sections.heading: Quarantine: scope, what actually stops allocation, and getting back out
sections.body:
A quarantine is scoped to whatever level the evidence supports. `farm.quarantines.scope` accepts `device`, `slot`, `power_domain`, `hub`, `host`; the ladder writes three of them — `device` (tier 6), `hub` (correlation), `host` (tier 8). Partial unique indexes enforce **one open quarantine per subject per scope**.

**A row in `farm.quarantines` alone stops nothing.** What the allocator consults is `farm.device_runtime.health = 'healthy'` and `farm.devices.admin_state = 'enabled'` (`farm.lease_acquire`), so every quarantine path also writes `health = 'quarantined'` for the devices in scope, in the same transaction. Get this wrong and you have a quarantine that pages a human and keeps handing the device out.

Live leases are untouched. Quarantine blocks **new** allocations; a job already on one of these devices keeps it, keeps its fence, and finishes on it.

Getting back out is a two-part protocol, and both parts must be running:

1. An operator closes the row: `POST /api/v1/quarantines/{id}/close`. A `reason` is mandatory — closing a quarantine claims the fault is fixed, and that claim is audited with the human's name.
2. The **ladder's next cycle** runs `reconcileQuarantines`, which finds devices at `health='quarantined'` with no open quarantine at any scope and drops them to `'unknown'` with `ladder_tier = 0`.

Back to `unknown` rather than `healthy` is deliberate: nobody has looked at the device since it was released, and `healthy` would be an assumption the allocator would act on. Resetting the ladder is equally deliberate — an operator who closes a quarantine has usually just fixed something, and resuming at rung 7 would answer their repair with an ADB server restart.

**The watchdog will not do this for you.** Its transition SQL has `WHEN c.cur_health IN ('retired','quarantined') THEN c.cur_health` — retirement is an administrative fact and quarantine belongs to the ladder, and neither is an observation the health loop may overwrite. If the recovery loop is not running, closing a quarantine leaves the devices stuck at `quarantined` and unschedulable indefinitely.

**Hysteresis on the way back.** Once a device is at `unknown`, the watchdog's flap damper decides how fast it returns to the pool. `flap_credits` is a token bucket (cap 10, refill 1/min), not a raw counter: going **down** to any non-healthy state is free but debounced by `consec_bad >= 2`; coming **up** to healthy costs one token *on top of* `consec_good >= 3`; from `unknown` specifically one good look is enough, but the token is still charged. The asymmetry is the mechanism — the expensive direction is the one that puts a bad device back in front of a tenant.

sections.heading: Bulk execution and the per-hub cap
sections.body:
`POST /api/v1/bulk` runs one shell command across a selector. `max_per_hub` is not a politeness knob: sixty devices answering at once browns out a power domain and produces a wave of transport errors that looks exactly like a hardware fault. Capping concurrency per hub keeps a bulk command from manufacturing the incident it was run to investigate.

The caps, in order:

- **`max_per_hub`** — default 4, clamped to 32. One buffered channel of that size per hub.
- **global 64** — forty hubs times four each is 160 simultaneous ADB sessions, which is a load test of the control plane rather than a bulk command.
- **`bulkSelectorLimit` = 1000** targets per run, reported as `truncated: true` rather than quietly shortened. An operator who believes a command reached the whole fleet when it reached the first thousand rows will draw a conclusion about the devices it never touched.
- **timeout** — default 30s per target, max 5 minutes. Output capped at 256 KiB, truncated rather than failed.

**Leased devices are skipped by default.** `include_leased` is off because a bulk shell across the farm that lands inside somebody's six-hour run is the most expensive mistake this endpoint can make. Skipped devices are recorded as `bulk_targets` rows in state `skipped` with the lease id in `error`, not dropped — the run says out loud what it declined to touch.

The run executes on the **server's background context**, not the request's: an operator closing their laptop must not abort a farm-wide command halfway. Shutdown asks it to stop, waits, then marks outstanding targets `skipped` with `the control plane shut down before this target ran` and the run `cancelled`.

Two implementation details that matter when things go wrong:

- Target inserts are **one statement each** (an `unnest` of parallel arrays), not one per device. A thousand sequential round trips would hold a pool connection and an open transaction for as long as they took — and that connection is one a lease renewal cannot borrow. A holder that cannot renew for ttl+grace loses its device. An operator's bulk command must never be able to squeeze the renewal path.
- On `ctx.Err()` the per-hub loop `break`s rather than `return`s, so `hubWG.Wait()` still runs. Returning would orphan in-flight goroutines and let shutdown stop waiting while they were still driving devices through a pool about to close.
bullets: Selector keys: `pool`, `host`, `hub` (matches `hub_path` or `hub_id`), `health`, `model` (ILIKE substring), `device`/`device_id` (repeatable, matches device_id or farm_uid), `include-leased`. Over the JSON API the field is `device_ids` (an array) and `include_leased`.

The CLI refuses `--selector host=` with an empty value and exits 2. An empty selector matches the whole farm — in practice that is `--selector host=$HOST` in a script where `HOST` never got set, and the result would be a reboot across every device in the building.

`ctl bulk` exits 1 if any target failed, even though the run itself completed. Exit 3 means the remote refused (HTTP 409) — an answer, not a crash. `--follow` defaults true; without it the command exits 0 regardless of outcome, because it never waits to find out.
Selection filters on `admin_state='enabled'` and on having an `adb_devpath` and `adb_endpoint`. It does **not** filter on health or quarantine — see gaps.

sections.heading: Operator actions and what they cost
sections.body:
Five endpoints in this area change state, and all five are gated by the `operator` role, require a non-empty `reason`, and write `farm.audit_log` on a context **detached from the request** — the state has already changed, so the record of who changed it must not depend on the caller still being connected. The read paths (`GET /api/v1/recovery`, `GET /api/v1/bulk`, `GET /api/v1/bulk/{id}`) are tenant-gated.

`handleSlotPower` refuses in four distinct ways, each recorded as a tier-4 `refused` attempt and audited: tier 4 disabled in `farm.recovery_tiers`; no controllable power domain (`power_domain_id IS NULL`, or `pd.control = 'none'`); hub `vbus_switchable = false`; or one or more live leases in the domain forbid it. In this seed the third is unreachable, because the only two hubs with `vbus_switchable=false` are exactly the two whose power domain has `control='none'`.

The drain response reads: `"no new leases will be placed on this host. The live leases above are untouched and will run to completion; nothing here releases them."` The second half is true. **The first half is not enforced anywhere** — read the gap before you rely on a drain. "Drained" meaning "I took eleven phones away from running jobs" is the failure this whole system is built against; "drained" meaning "nothing changed" is the failure this endpoint currently has.

rows: evaluates tier 4 for the slot's power domain; on approval records an open attempt row, audits, emits `slot_power_requested`
does not toggle VBUS itself, does not touch any lease, and nothing ever closes the attempt row it opens
sets `farm.hosts.admin_state='draining'`, counts live and protected leases, audits
does not end the live leases — and does not stop new ones either: no allocation path reads this column
closes the row, audits with the operator's name and reason
does not make devices schedulable on its own — the ladder's `reconcileQuarantines` does that, and only if it is running
creates a run and its target rows, then executes on the server's background context
does not touch leased devices unless `include_leased` is set; does not skip quarantined or unhealthy ones

sections.heading: Reading it back at 3am
sections.body:
Three questions, three queries.

**"Why is this device not getting fixed?"** — filter `farm.recovery_attempts` on `outcome='refused'` and read `refusal`. That column exists so the UI can explain a gap instead of showing one. Remember it misses host-agent refusals, which land as `outcome='failed'` with the text in `detail->>'refusal'`.

**"Is the ladder working, or is my fleet's disruption policy stopping it?"** — group attempts by tier and outcome. A wall of `refused` at tier 4 means the policies your tenants are writing, not a broken ladder. A total absence of tiers 1, 2, 3, 5 and 7 means the ladder's per-device path has never run at all.

**"What is quarantined, and did anyone look at it?"** — `farm.quarantines WHERE closed_at IS NULL`, joined against `farm.audit_log`. Do not use `farm.v_fleet.quarantine_reason`: it only resolves device-scoped quarantines.

On metrics, be careful about what is actually exported. The registry receives only `obs.Register(reg)` (`cmd/farmd/roles.go:80`), so for recovery you get:

- `farm_recovery_attempts_total{host,hub,rack_slot,tier,outcome}` — the obs version, with physical position labels and a deliberately coarse five-value `tier` label (`reprobe`, `reconnect`, `soft_reset`, `port_power_cycle`, `quarantine`) so a retuned ladder cannot multiply time series.
- `farm_api_operator_actions_total{action,outcome}` — covers `slot.power`, `quarantine.close`, `host.drain`, `host.undrain`, `bulk.create`, `lease.revoke`, `job.cancel`, `artifact.delete`.
- `farm_api_bulk_targets_total{outcome}` — ok / error / skipped.
- `farm_device_health{host,hub,state}` — the gauge behind the fleet grid.

The ladder's own counters (`farm_recovery_refusals_total`, `farm_recovery_budget_skips_total`, `farm_recovery_hub_quarantines_total`, `farm_recovery_quarantines_cleared_total`, `farm_recovery_candidates`, `farm_recovery_cycles_total`, `farm_recovery_heartbeat_failures_total`) are **defined but never registered**, and cannot simply be registered — see gaps.

sections.heading: Reading this demo's data honestly
sections.body:
This page's examples come from the running demo, which is 56 simulated devices on two fake ADB servers driven by the real control plane. The hardware is fake; the scheduler, lease store, reaper, watchdog and recovery ladder are production code paths.

But `farm.recovery_attempts` on this demo has three authors, and they are easy to confuse.

- **`internal/recovery/ladder.go`** — the real ladder. On this demo its entire output is three hub-correlation rows at tier 6 (`{"scope":"hub","devices":…,"window_s":…,"quarantine_id":…}`, NULL device_id and slot_id) plus the quarantines they opened. Zero per-device attempts, zero ladder refusals.
- **`internal/api/ops.go`** — every `POST /slots/{id}/power`. Refusals carry `{"vbus_switchable":…}` or `{"offenders":[…]}`; approvals carry the full domain context and stay open forever.
- **`internal/demo/demo.go`** — the simulator, which writes its own tier-0 and tier-4 rows to narrate the STF #663 scenario. Its detail shape is `{"considered":"port_power"}` or `{"self_healed":true,"tier":0}`, and its refusal texts are its own.

The reason the real ladder so rarely acts here is the 45-second debounce: the simulator restores its offline devices well inside that window, so they never become candidates. Only hub 4-2 on h02, which is seeded permanently faulty, stays broken long enough — and it is hub-correlated, so the per-device path is skipped for it too.

What this demo does prove: the blast-radius refusal path, the audit trail, quarantine and reconciliation, bulk execution and its caps, and the invariant itself. What it does not prove: that tiers 1, 2, 3, 5 and 7 work, because none of them has ever executed.

                          OR detail ? 'self_healed')  AS demo_simulator,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE detail ? 'requested_by'
                          OR detail ? 'offenders'
                          OR detail ? 'vbus_switchable') AS api_slot_power

gaps.what: `POST /api/v1/hosts/{id}/drain` is not enforced by the allocator. It sets `farm.hosts.admin_state='draining'` and returns "no new leases will be placed on this host", but `farm.lease_acquire` never reads that column. A grep of the whole tree finds three readers of `farm.hosts.admin_state`: the drain handler reading its own previous value, `cmd/farmd/roles.go:221` and the ladder's candidate query — the last two compare against `'disabled'` only. The value `'draining'` is written and never acted upon.
gaps.consequence: An operator drains a host before physical work and believes jobs have stopped landing on it. They have not. Verified live: h02 was drained at 11:00:08 and seven new leases were acquired on it in the following sixty seconds, while `admin_state` read `draining` throughout. Until this is fixed, the only mechanism that actually stops allocation to a host is a host-scoped quarantine (recovery tier 8, or a manual row plus `health='quarantined'`), because that writes the column the allocator reads.

gaps.what: No shipped deployment wires a `HostRunner` into the recovery ladder, so tiers 3 (usb_reset) and 4 (port_power) never execute. `cmd/farmd/roles.go:206` constructs `recovery.NewADBActuator(log, nil)` unconditionally for the `recovery`, `all` and `demo` roles alike. `farmd node` serves POST /node/v1/usb-reset and /node/v1/port-power, but nothing in the tree is an HTTP client for those routes and no role runs the agent and the ladder in one process.
gaps.consequence: The ladder climbs: tier 3 fails, tier 4 fails, tier 5 (device_reboot, ADB-reachable) runs, tier 6 quarantines. A device whose USB link a reset would have fixed reaches quarantine roughly two rungs early, and the operator gets a page for hardware that was recoverable. To get tiers 3 and 4 you must write the seam yourself.

gaps.what: A host-agent refusal is recorded as `outcome='failed'` with the `refusal` column left NULL. `ADBActuator.hostLocal` returns `OutcomeRefused`, but `Ladder.perform`'s switch only passes through recovered/no_change/failed and maps anything else to `OutcomeFailed`, putting the text in `detail.refusal` and `detail.actuator_outcome` instead.
gaps.consequence: `WHERE outcome='refused'` — the obvious query, and the one the dashboard's refusal column uses via `recoveryAttempts` — silently misses every missing-host-agent and platform-unsupported refusal. You have to read `detail->>'refusal'` on failed rows too.

gaps.what: Nothing consumes the tier-4 attempt row that an approved `POST /api/v1/slots/{id}/power` writes. The response says "the host agent performs the switch and closes recovery attempt N with its outcome"; no code anywhere reads `farm.recovery_attempts`.
gaps.consequence: Verified live: three rows (65, 94, 98) sit open with NULL outcome, the oldest for 28 minutes and counting. Each shows in the `recovery_open` index and in `GET /api/v1/recovery` as a ladder still climbing. They also consume one of the tier's four hourly budget slots for that power domain for an hour each — the ladder's own CTE returned `in_hour=2` for domain 1 — though not permanently, and they never block the in-flight check because that keys on `device_id`, which this path leaves NULL.

gaps.what: `recovery.Collectors()` and `node.Collectors()` are never registered, and `recovery.Collectors()` cannot be registered as it stands: `recovery.attemptsTotal` and `obs.recoveryAttempts` both resolve to the fully-qualified name `farm_recovery_attempts_total` with different label sets and different help strings.
gaps.consequence: Reproduced against a fresh registry with both descriptors verbatim: the second registration returns "a previously registered descriptor with the same fully-qualified name ... has different label names or a different help string". Because `newRegistry` propagates the error, adding `recovery.Collectors()` to the binary makes farmd fail to start. So `farm_recovery_refusals_total{tier,kind}` — the only series that distinguishes refused_ganged from refused_policy — plus `budget_skips_total{tier,reason}`, `hub_quarantines_total`, `quarantines_cleared_total`, `candidates`, `cycles_total` and `heartbeat_failures_total` are absent from /metrics, and the fix is a rename, not a one-line registration. Verified: grep for those names on the live /metrics returns 0 matches. You cannot alert on a ladder that is skipping every attempt on budget.

gaps.what: `obs.OutcomeRefusedGanged` is never emitted in practice. Its only producer is `recovery.recordRefusal`, which requires the ladder's per-device path to run; `internal/demo/demo.go` hardcodes `obs.OutcomeRefusedPolicy` even for its own ganged refusals.
gaps.consequence: The documented signal "a rising refused_ganged rate means the rack needs per-port power switching" is not available. Live `/metrics` carries exactly three outcome values: recovered, failed, refused_policy. Until the ladder's per-device path runs and its own collectors are registerable, ganged refusals are indistinguishable from policy refusals in metrics — you have to go to `farm.recovery_attempts.refusal` text.

gaps.what: The `farmd node` role cannot start on any GOOS but Linux, and it defeats the per-host heartbeat key. `runNode` calls `topo.Sysfs("/sys")` before constructing the agent, and `internal/topo/sysfs.go` returns an error on non-Linux. Separately, `runNode` passes `Component: "node"` explicitly, overriding `internal/node`'s `node:<host id>` default.
gaps.consequence: The package doc's promise that the agent "still runs" on other platforms describes `internal/node`, not the shipped binary — a developer following it will get a startup error, not a graceful ErrNotSupported. And in a multi-host fleet every agent writes the same `farm.component_heartbeat` row, so one healthy host's beat hides a dead host — exactly the failure the doc comment says the per-host key exists to prevent.

gaps.what: `farm.v_fleet` joins quarantines with `q.device_id = d.id`, so only device-scoped quarantines appear. Hub- and host-scoped quarantines have `device_id` NULL.
gaps.consequence: Verified live: seven devices on hub 8 read `health='quarantined'` in `farm.v_fleet` with `quarantine_id` and `quarantine_reason` both NULL, while a hub-scoped quarantine for hub 8 was open. The fleet grid shows a quarantined device with no explanation; you have to query `farm.quarantines` yourself.

gaps.what: `farm.v_hub_health.unhealthy` and the ladder's correlation numerator are different definitions. The view counts `health NOT IN ('healthy','retired')` — which includes quarantined, unknown and recovering; `unhealthyPredicate` counts only offline, unauthorized, missing, degraded.
gaps.consequence: Verified live: the view reads 7/7 unhealthy for hub 8 at the same moment the correlate query reads 0/7, because all seven are quarantined. The fleet banner and the quarantine reason on the same hub will report different counts, and neither is wrong. Any alert threshold written against the view is not the threshold the ladder uses.

gaps.what: Closing a quarantine has no effect unless the recovery loop is running. `handleQuarantineClose` only updates `farm.quarantines`; the health write that actually makes devices schedulable lives in the ladder's `reconcileQuarantines`, and the watchdog's transition SQL explicitly refuses to overwrite `health='quarantined'`.
gaps.consequence: If the recovery role is down, an operator can close every quarantine in the fleet and no device comes back. The API returns 200 either way. Verified by timing: the close returned immediately at 10:55:25, the devices were still `quarantined` at 10:55:33, and only the next ladder cycle (10:55:41) moved them to `unknown`.

gaps.what: `handleQuarantineClose` does not restore `farm.devices.admin_state`. `reconcileQuarantines` only writes `farm.device_runtime.health`, and nothing in `internal/recovery` reads or writes `admin_state='quarantined'` — a value the schema permits and `internal/demo/demo.go` writes.
gaps.consequence: Any path that parks a device at `admin_state='quarantined'` outside the demo's own paired closer leaves it permanently unschedulable, because `farm.lease_acquire` requires `d.admin_state='enabled'` and the ladder's candidate query requires it too — so the device is also invisible to recovery. The API close will report success and change nothing for it. Today only the demo writes that value, so this is latent rather than active.

gaps.what: `acknowledged` is never populated by any caller. `ADBActuator` tier 4 calls `HostRunner.PortPower(...)`, which is `PortPowerWithDomain(..., nil)`. Only the HTTP node endpoint accepts the field, and nothing sends it.
gaps.consequence: On a ganged hub with any other occupied port, `checkBlastRadius` in the agent will refuse tier 4 unconditionally — even after the control plane has verified that every lease in the domain permits it. Tier 4 on ganged hardware is effectively unavailable through the in-process seam.

gaps.what: Tier 0 (`observe`) is unreachable through the ladder. `ladder_tier` defaults to 0 (`migrations/00001_core.sql:207`) and is only ever set to 0 or to a tier that was attempted, and `next(tiers, cur)` returns the first rung with `tier > cur`.
gaps.consequence: The ladder's first action on a settled unhealthy device is tier 1 (adb_reconnect), not tier 0. The "do nothing for one debounce window" behaviour still happens — it comes from `DefaultDebounce` (45s) plus the watchdog's `consec_bad >= 2` — but the tier table advertises a rung that never runs and a 60/hour budget that is never spent. On this demo the 54 tier-0 rows in `farm.recovery_attempts` were all written by the simulator, so the table looks busy at a rung the ladder cannot reach.

gaps.what: `farm.quarantines.scope` permits `slot` and `power_domain`, and there is a partial unique index for `slot`, but no code writes either. There is no `power_domain_id` column at all, so a power-domain quarantine has no way to name its subject, and the ladder's candidate query does not check for one.
gaps.consequence: A hub with mixed per-port and ganged domains cannot be quarantined at the granularity of the actual fault. The choice is one device or the whole hub.

gaps.what: Bulk selection does not exclude quarantined or unhealthy devices. `expandBulkSelector` filters only on `adb_devpath IS NOT NULL`, `adb_endpoint IS NOT NULL` and `admin_state='enabled'`.
gaps.consequence: Verified live: a run against h02 hit all seven devices of the quarantined hub 4-2, five of which errored on transport. Harmless for a read-only getprop; a `reboot` or an install across a selector that happens to include a quarantined hub will produce a wave of failures and a misleading error rate. Add `health=healthy` to the selector when you mean healthy devices.

gaps.what: In this demo's seed, all seven slots of every hub share one `power_domain_id`, including hubs whose `power_domains.kind` is `per_port`.
gaps.consequence: Tier 4's blast radius is the whole hub even on per-port hardware, so any neighbour's `no_disruption` lease refuses a cycle that would physically have disturbed only one port. Verified in the live 409: `power_kind: per_port`, `slots_in_domain: 7`, refused because of one lease on a different slot. Whether this is right depends on how you model your own rack — but if you model a per-port hub as one domain, you get conservative refusals and a refusal rate that has nothing to do with your hardware.

gaps.what: `GET /api/v1/recovery` has no filter for outcome, tier or time. It takes `device`, `host` and `limit` (default 100, max 1000) and returns the most recent attempts.
gaps.consequence: The 3am question — "show me every refusal at tier 4 in the last hour" — cannot be asked through the API or the dashboard. You have to go to psql. The `refusal` column exists so the UI can explain a gap; the endpoint does not let you find the gap.

gaps.what: On this demo the recovery ladder's per-device escalation path has never executed: zero rows in `farm.recovery_attempts` carry `begin`'s detail shape, and tiers 1, 2, 3, 5, 7 and 8 have no rows at all. The simulator restores its offline devices inside the 45-second debounce, and the one permanently faulty hub is handled by correlation, which skips the per-device loop.
gaps.consequence: Nothing you can observe on this demo is evidence that `ADBActuator`'s ADB rungs work end to end, that `recordRefusal` writes what it claims, or that the budget skips fire. Treat the demo as proof of the refusal contract, the audit trail, quarantine reconciliation and bulk execution — not of the ladder's actuator path.
